terms.label: A/B test
terms.definition: A controlled experiment that randomly splits users into a control group and one or more treatment groups, then compares an outcome metric between them.

terms.label: p-value
terms.definition: The probability of seeing a result at least as extreme as the one observed if there were truly no effect. It is not the probability that the result is a fluke.

terms.label: Lift
terms.definition: The relative improvement of the treatment over control on a metric, for example (treatment minus control) divided by control.

terms.label: Statistical significance
terms.definition: A result is called significant when its p-value falls below a threshold chosen in advance, commonly 0.05. It says the data would be unlikely if there were no effect, not that the effect is large or important.

terms.label: Type I error
terms.definition: A false positive: concluding there is an effect when there isn't one. The significance level sets how often you accept this.

terms.label: Type II error
terms.definition: A false negative: missing an effect that is really there. Its rate is one minus the test's power.

terms.label: Sample size
terms.definition: How many observations an experiment needs to reliably detect an effect of a chosen size. It depends on the baseline rate, the variance, and the error rates you accept.

terms.label: Default rate
terms.definition: The share of borrowers who fail to repay a loan within a defined period.

terms.label: Confidence interval
terms.definition: A range computed with a procedure that, over many repeated studies, would contain the true value a stated share of the time, for example 95%.

terms.label: Bootstrapping
terms.definition: Estimating uncertainty by repeatedly resampling your own data with replacement and recomputing a statistic each time.

terms.label: Simpson's paradox
terms.definition: A pattern where a trend that appears in several subgroups reverses or disappears when the groups are combined.

terms.label: Customer segment
terms.definition: A group of customers treated as similar for analysis, for example by size, region or behavior.

terms.label: XGBoost
terms.definition: A popular gradient-boosting library that builds many small decision trees in sequence, each one correcting the errors of the ones before it.

terms.label: Gradient boosting
terms.definition: An ensemble method that adds models one at a time, each trained to reduce the error that remains in the combined model so far.

terms.label: Logistic regression
terms.definition: A linear model for classification that outputs a probability. It is simple, fast and easy to explain.

terms.label: AUC
terms.definition: Area under the ROC curve: the chance that the model scores a random positive example above a random negative one. 0.5 is chance and 1.0 is perfect ranking.

terms.label: Test set
terms.definition: Data held back from training and used only to estimate how the model will perform on new data.

terms.label: Model in production
terms.definition: A model serving real predictions to real users or downstream systems, as opposed to being evaluated offline.

terms.label: Model drift
terms.definition: Decline in a deployed model's performance over time because the world, or the data it sees, has changed since it was trained.

terms.label: Model degradation
terms.definition: A measurable drop in a deployed model's quality compared with when it launched, whatever the cause.

terms.label: Model monitoring
terms.definition: Tracking a deployed model's inputs, predictions and outcomes to catch problems early.

terms.label: Alerting
terms.definition: Automatic notifications when a monitored value crosses a threshold, so someone can act.

terms.label: Cash collection forecast
terms.definition: A prediction of when, and how much of, the money owed on invoices will actually be received.

terms.label: Cash flow forecast
terms.definition: A prediction of the money coming in and going out over a future period.

terms.label: Forecast horizon
terms.definition: How far into the future a forecast looks, for example 90 days or 12 months. Accuracy generally worsens as the horizon grows.

terms.label: Forecasting
terms.definition: Predicting future values of a quantity from past data and known drivers.

terms.label: Time series
terms.definition: Data recorded over time in order, where the sequence matters because observations are usually related to nearby ones.

terms.label: Backtesting
terms.definition: Evaluating a forecasting method by replaying history: at each past date, use only what was known then, predict forward, and compare with what happened.

terms.label: Cross-validation
terms.definition: Estimating performance by training and evaluating on several different splits of the data and averaging the results.

terms.label: k-fold
terms.definition: A cross-validation scheme that splits the data into k parts and takes turns holding each one out for evaluation.

terms.label: Feature engineering
terms.definition: Turning raw data into inputs a model can learn from, such as ratios, counts over a time window or encoded categories.

terms.label: Feature importance
terms.definition: A score for how much each input feature contributes to a model's predictions. Different methods can rank the same features differently.

terms.label: Data pipeline
terms.definition: A sequence of automated steps that moves data from its sources, transforms it, and delivers it for use, such as model training.

terms.label: Data validation
terms.definition: Automated checks that data meets expectations (types, ranges, missing values, freshness) before it is used.

terms.label: Data quality
terms.definition: How well data fits its purpose: accurate, complete, consistent, timely and free of unwanted duplicates.

terms.label: Churn
terms.definition: When a customer stops using or paying for a product. The churn rate is the share lost in a period.

terms.label: Cohort
terms.definition: A group of users who share a starting point, typically the period they signed up, tracked together over time.

terms.label: Retention
terms.definition: The share of a group that is still active some time after they started.

terms.label: Window function
terms.definition: A SQL function that computes a value for each row using a set of related rows (its window) without collapsing them into one row.

terms.label: Top N per group
terms.definition: A common SQL pattern: keep only the N highest-ranked rows within each group, such as each department.

terms.label: Rolling average
terms.definition: An average over a sliding window of recent values, used to smooth out day-to-day noise.

terms.label: Sessionization
terms.definition: Grouping a stream of user events into sessions, usually by starting a new one after a long enough gap.

terms.label: Anti-join
terms.definition: A query that returns the rows in one table that have no match in another.

terms.label: pandas merge
terms.definition: Combining two DataFrames on matching key columns, like a SQL join.

terms.label: Duplicate records
terms.definition: Multiple rows that refer to the same real-world entity. What counts as a duplicate depends on the business definition.

terms.label: Bias-variance tradeoff
terms.definition: The tension between a model too simple to capture the pattern (bias) and one so flexible that it fits noise in the training data (variance).

terms.label: Evaluation metric
terms.definition: A number that summarizes how well a model performs, such as accuracy, precision, recall or AUC. Each one rewards different behavior.

terms.label: Accuracy
terms.definition: The share of predictions that are correct.

terms.label: Fraud detection
terms.definition: Identifying transactions or accounts that are deliberately deceptive. Fraud is rare, and fraudsters adapt.

terms.label: Missing data
terms.definition: Values that are absent from a dataset. Why they are missing affects how they should be handled.

terms.label: Outliers
terms.definition: Values far from the rest of the data. They can be errors or genuinely rare events.

terms.label: Experimentation platform
terms.definition: Shared infrastructure that assigns users to experiment variants, logs exposure and reports results, so teams can run A/B tests consistently.

terms.label: Batch processing
terms.definition: Computing over accumulated data on a schedule, such as nightly.

terms.label: Stream processing
terms.definition: Computing on events continuously as they arrive.

terms.label: Feature pipeline
terms.definition: The data flow that computes the inputs a model uses, both for training and for live predictions.

terms.label: Real-time
terms.definition: Responding within a tight latency bound, typically milliseconds to a few seconds, as each request arrives.

terms.label: Recommendation system
terms.definition: A system that suggests items a user is likely to want, using their history and the behavior of similar users.

terms.label: ML intake process
terms.definition: The way a company collects, evaluates, prioritizes and approves requests for machine learning work.

terms.label: Algorithmic fairness
terms.definition: Whether a model's decisions treat groups of people equitably. There are several competing definitions, and they cannot all be satisfied at once.

terms.label: Disparate impact
terms.definition: When a decision process affects one group at a materially different rate than another, even without using a protected attribute directly.

terms.label: Model rollout
terms.definition: Moving a new model into live use, from limited exposure up to full traffic.

terms.label: Unit test
terms.definition: An automated test of one small piece of code against an expected result.

terms.label: Training-serving skew
terms.definition: A mismatch between how features are computed or distributed during training and during live prediction.

terms.label: Reproducibility
terms.definition: Being able to rerun an analysis or model and obtain the same result.

terms.label: Model serving
terms.definition: Running a trained model so that other systems can request predictions from it.

terms.label: Latency
terms.definition: The time between a request and its response.

terms.label: Memory footprint
terms.definition: How much RAM a program needs while it runs.

terms.label: RAG
terms.definition: Retrieval-augmented generation: look up relevant documents first, then give them to a language model to base its answer on.

terms.label: LLM evaluation
terms.definition: Measuring how good a language-model application's outputs are, often with rubrics, human labels or another model acting as judge.

terms.label: Prompt engineering
terms.definition: Shaping a language model's behavior by changing its instructions and examples, without changing the model itself.

terms.label: Fine-tuning
terms.definition: Further training a pre-trained model on your own examples so that its behavior or style changes.

terms.label: Hallucination
terms.definition: When a language model states something fluent and confident that is false or unsupported.

terms.label: AI agent
terms.definition: A language-model system that decides for itself which tools to call and which steps to take toward a goal.

terms.label: Tool calling
terms.definition: A model asking for external code to run, such as a search or database query, and then using the result.

terms.label: JSON
terms.definition: A text format for structured data using key-value pairs and arrays.

terms.label: Token
terms.definition: A chunk of text, often a word fragment, that a language model reads and generates one at a time.

terms.label: Temperature
terms.definition: A sampling setting on LLM requests, usually between 0 and 2.

terms.label: Top-p
terms.definition: Another sampling setting on LLM requests, between 0 and 1.

terms.label: System prompt
terms.definition: Instructions given to a language model ahead of the user's input to set its behavior.

terms.label: Chunk
terms.definition: A segment of a document split out for indexing and retrieval.

terms.label: Ground truth
terms.definition: The verified correct answers against which a system's outputs are compared.

terms.label: Precision and recall
terms.definition: Precision is the share of predicted positives that are correct. Recall is the share of actual positives that were found.

terms.label: Validation set
terms.definition: Data held out from training and used to evaluate a model while it is being developed.

terms.label: Random forest
terms.definition: An ensemble of decision trees, each trained on a random sample of the data, whose predictions are combined.

terms.label: Predicted probability
terms.definition: The number between 0 and 1 that a classifier outputs for how likely a case is to be positive.

terms.label: High cardinality
terms.definition: Describes a feature with a very large number of distinct values.

terms.label: Multicollinearity
terms.definition: When two or more input features are strongly correlated with each other.

terms.label: Decision threshold
terms.definition: The score above which a model's output is treated as a positive prediction.

terms.label: Residual
terms.definition: The difference between an observed value and the model's prediction for it.

terms.label: R-squared
terms.definition: The share of variance in the outcome that a regression model explains.

terms.label: Training data
terms.definition: The historical examples a model learns from.

terms.label: Retraining
terms.definition: Fitting a model again on newer data to replace the version in production.

terms.label: PSI
terms.definition: Population Stability Index: a score that compares the binned distribution of a variable between two periods.

terms.label: Feature store
terms.definition: A shared system that stores, computes and serves model input features.

terms.label: Human review
terms.definition: A step in which a person checks or overrides a model's output before action is taken.

terms.label: Data structure
terms.definition: A way of organizing data in memory so it can be accessed or changed efficiently.

terms.label: DataFrame
terms.definition: A table of rows and labeled columns, as used in pandas.

terms.label: Default argument
terms.definition: A value a function parameter takes when the caller does not supply one.

terms.label: Parallelism
terms.definition: Running several computations at the same time on separate CPU cores or machines.

terms.label: Ranking
terms.definition: Ordering rows by a value and assigning each a position, such as 1st or 2nd.

terms.label: Aggregate function
terms.definition: A function such as COUNT, SUM or AVG that collapses many rows into one value.

terms.label: Growth rate
terms.definition: The change in a metric between two periods, usually shown as a percentage of the earlier period.

terms.label: Streak
terms.definition: A run of consecutive days (or other periods) with the same behavior.

terms.label: Join
terms.definition: An operation that combines rows from two tables using a matching condition.

terms.label: NULL
terms.definition: A marker meaning a value is missing or unknown. It is not the same as zero or an empty string.

terms.label: Median
terms.definition: The middle value when observations are sorted: half the values fall below it and half above.

terms.label: Repeat purchase rate
terms.definition: The share of customers who buy more than once.

terms.label: Central limit theorem
terms.definition: A theorem in probability about the averages of samples.

terms.label: Mean
terms.definition: The arithmetic average: the sum of values divided by how many there are.

terms.label: Frequentist
terms.definition: An approach to inference in which probability describes long-run frequencies across repeated experiments.

terms.label: Causation
terms.definition: A relationship in which changing one variable produces a change in another, rather than the two merely moving together.

terms.label: Control group
terms.definition: The subjects who do not receive the treatment, used as the comparison for those who do.

terms.label: Standard error
terms.definition: A measure of how much a statistic, such as a sample mean, would vary across repeated samples.

terms.label: Anomaly detection
terms.definition: Identifying observations that deviate markedly from the expected pattern.

terms.label: Scenario analysis
terms.definition: Examining how an outcome changes under different sets of assumptions.

terms.label: Embedding
terms.definition: A list of numbers representing a piece of text (or other data) so that similar items sit close together.
